strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Use a constrained, population-based differential-evolution search that evaluates the exact minimax objective for every candidate. Keep the validated supplied construction as an initial population member and as an independent fallback. Differential mutation combines coordinated differences between feasible population members; binomial crossover creates additional directions; a joint box-and-sum projection restores feasibility before scoring. Adapt mutation and crossover settings from successful proposals, maintain an archive of replaced solutions, and trigger a small fixed number of diversity restarts after explicit stagnation thresholds.

This is materially different from an epigraph/SLSQP search, a smoothed projected-gradient search, and a pairwise-coordinate line search: the proposed method uses no epigraph, gradient, smooth surrogate, or one-dimensional pair minimization. It searches with population-level stochastic vector mutations and exact score-based selection. The justified facts are that the evaluator is a maximum over all 2n−1 finite-support correlation values, that differences of feasible vectors have zero sum, and that projection onto the box intersected with the fixed-sum hyperplane is computable by a scalar threshold. The hypothesis is that coordinated mutations, population diversity, and restarts may find a better basin than the supplied local search. The objective remains nonconvex; this method offers no guarantee of improvement, of reaching 0.3808, or of finding a global optimum. Exact evaluator scores, not a proxy, determine every retained solution.

2. Mathematical specification

For resolution n, let dx=2/n, S=n/2, and h=(h[0],…,h[n−1]). The feasible set is K={h: 0≤h[i]≤1 for all i, sum_i h[i]=S}. Keep the valid parent’s resolution fixed; if there is no valid parent, use n=45. All vectors are float64.

For each integer lag s from −(n−1) through n−1, define
Q_s(h)=sum_{i=max(0,−s)}^{min(n,n−s)−1} h[i](1−h[i+s]),
where the upper limit is exclusive. This is a finite-support, non-wrapping overlap: only indices for which both entries exist contribute. The exact score is
C(h)=dx·max_s Q_s(h)=max(np.correlate(h,1−h,mode='full'))·(2/n).
The correlation output has length 2n−1; its lag ordering may reverse the displayed s ordering, but the maximum over all lags is unchanged. Include both lag directions and the partial-overlap boundary terms. Do not replace this objective with circular correlation or with an autocorrelation identity that drops boundary terms.

For any finite vector v, the Euclidean projection onto K is y[i]=clip(v[i]−λ,0,1), where λ solves sum_i clip(v[i]−λ,0,1)=S. The sum is continuous and nonincreasing in λ. A scalar bisection followed by residual correction through remaining box capacity gives a joint box-and-sum feasibility mechanism; clipping and then rescaling is not valid.

In generation g, population member x_i belongs to K. Choose a p-best member x_p from the best-ranked fraction of the population, a distinct population member x_r1, and x_r2 from the population or an archive of feasible replaced members. The current-to-pbest/1 donor is
v_i=x_i+F_i(x_p−x_i)+F_i(x_r1−x_r2).
Each difference has sum zero, so the donor has sum S, although it may violate box bounds. Binomial crossover chooses each coordinate from v_i or x_i, forcing at least one donor coordinate; crossover can change the sum. Project the crossed vector onto K before evaluating it.

There is no convex or differentiable subproblem and no external optimizer. This is a derivative-free heuristic on the original objective. Accept a projected trial only when its exact C score is strictly lower than its target member’s exact score by the stated numerical tolerance. Use exact scores for population ranking, global-best storage, restart decisions, and final return.

3. Implementation procedure

1) Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) and all helpers as top-level functions; do not use closures or lambdas. Use only permitted NumPy and math functionality. Do not use filesystem or network I/O. Seed np.random.default_rng(seed); if seed conversion or generator creation fails, use seed 42. Ignore unused kwargs. Do not use CVXPY or a gradient-based solver for this nonconvex objective.

2) Implement check_feasible(h,n). Convert only a copy to float64. Require a one-dimensional vector of length n, finite entries, every entry in [0,1], and abs(sum(h)−n/2)≤1e−10·max(1,n). Implement exact_score(h,n) to return positive infinity if that check fails or an exception occurs; otherwise compute np.correlate(h,1.0−h,mode='full'), require a finite result of length 2n−1, and return float(max(correlation)*(2.0/n)). This is the authoritative score helper; do not substitute an FFT approximation, a surrogate, or the pre-imported evaluator for it.

3) Implement project_box_sum(v,S). Reject a non-1D or nonfinite input, an empty vector, or S outside [0,n]. Set lo=min(v)−1 and hi=max(v); at lo the clipped sum is n, and at hi it is zero. Perform 100 bisection steps, moving lo upward when sum(clip(v−mid,0,1))>S and hi downward otherwise. Set y=clip(v−(lo+hi)/2,0,1). Compute r=S−sum(y). If r>0, visit coordinates in decreasing order of available capacity 1−y[i], adding at most min(r,1−y[i]); if r<0, visit in decreasing order of capacity y[i] and subtract at most min(−r,y[i]). Recompute the residual after adjustments. Stop when its magnitude is at most 1e−12·max(1,n); return failure if remaining capacity cannot meet this tolerance. Require finite values, strict box bounds, and the check_feasible sum tolerance before returning. This projection is used for all generated candidates that are not already retained as a validated parent.

4) Read the optional parent using globals().get('initial_h_values',None). Do not redefine it, serialize its entries, or mutate its supplied array. Make a float64 copy. Accept it only when it is one-dimensional, has 2≤n≤999 entries, is finite, lies within [−1e−8,1+1e−8], and its sum differs from n/2 by at most 1e−6·max(1,n). If it already passes check_feasible, retain that copy directly. Otherwise clip only its admitted tiny box deviations, apply project_box_sum, and require the repaired result to pass check_feasible. This repaired or directly validated vector is the parent, an initial population member, and a preserved fallback. Do not change its n. If the parent is absent, malformed, or cannot be repaired, set n=45 and use np.full(45,0.5) as both parent fallback and initial feasible vector.

5) Select fixed search limits from n: for n≤64 use population size P=96, generation limit G=300, stagnation limit 50, and at most 3 restarts; for 65≤n≤128 use P=56, G=150, stagnation limit 30, and at most 2 restarts; for n>128 use P=20, G=32, stagnation limit 10, and at most 1 restart. In all cases use p_fraction=0.20, parameter adaptation rate c=0.10, initial mean mutation factor mu_F=0.55, and initial mean crossover rate mu_CR=0.70. These constants and all loops must be in the generated program.

6) Build the initial population algorithmically. Start with the parent copy itself. Offer its complement 1−parent, its reversal, and np.roll(parent,1), projecting each candidate with project_box_sum. Offer parent plus independent Gaussian noise at standard deviations 0.03, 0.08, 0.18, and 0.35, each projected. Add projected rng.random(n) candidates. Add harmonic candidates using idx=np.arange(n): for m=1,…,min(4,floor(n/2)), draw phases phi and theta from the seeded generator and form u=0.5+0.28*cos(2πm·idx/n+phi)+0.12*sin(2π(m+1)·idx/n+theta); project u. These formulas are algorithmic constructions, not stored tables.

Implement a top-level helper that projects a proposed start, checks feasibility, and appends it only if its maximum absolute coordinate difference from every current member is at least 1e−10. Add candidates in the order above, stopping when P unique members have been collected. Fill remaining slots by alternating between a projected parent perturbation with sigma drawn uniformly from [0.03,0.35] and a projected rng.random(n) vector. Allow at most 30P fill attempts; if uniqueness still prevents filling P slots, append feasible copies of the parent. Score all P members with exact_score. If a start unexpectedly receives an invalid score, replace it with a parent copy and score that. Initialize global_best_h and global_best_score from the parent and all finite-scoring population members, retaining copies. Keep the parent fallback separately even if another member is better.

7) For each generation, use a synchronous update. Copy the current population and scores as the immutable generation snapshot; make separate next-population and next-score copies. Rank the snapshot by score using np.argsort. Let top_count=max(2,ceil(p_fraction·P)). For target i, choose pbest uniformly from the top_count indices excluding i if any are available; otherwise choose from the top set. Choose r1 uniformly from population indices excluding i and pbest. Choose r2 uniformly from the remaining population indices excluding i, pbest, and r1, together with every archive entry. If the archive is empty, choose only from the remaining population indices. P is always at least 20, so these population choices are nonempty.

8) Sample mutation and crossover parameters per target. For F_i, sample a Cauchy variate mu_F+0.1·tan(π(U−0.5)), with U drawn uniformly and bounded away from 0 and 1. Retry up to 10 times if the result is not positive; if all retries fail use mu_F. Clip the result to [0.05,1]. Sample CR_i from a normal distribution with mean mu_CR and standard deviation 0.1, then clip to [0,1]. Form the donor v_i with the section 2 formula. Draw a binomial coordinate mask with probability CR_i and force a uniformly selected coordinate jrand to use the donor. Start the crossed trial as a copy of x_i and replace its masked coordinates by the corresponding donor coordinates. Project this crossed vector with project_box_sum; skip it if projection or feasibility checking fails. Compute its exact score and skip any nonfinite score.

9) Accept a trial for target i only when
score_trial < score_i−1e−14·max(1,abs(score_i)).
For an accepted trial, place it and its score in the next population, and append a copy of the replaced target to a generation-local archive. Otherwise retain the target unchanged. Compare every accepted trial’s exact score with the global-best score and copy it into global_best_h on strict improvement. After processing all targets, commit the next population and scores. Cap the archive at P by repeatedly deleting a uniformly random archive entry; archive entries are feasible replaced targets. Use the archive as it existed at the beginning of the generation for all r2 choices, so a synchronous generation is independent of the order in which targets are processed.

10) Adapt means only from accepted trials. If the generation has successful F values, set mu_F=0.9·mu_F+0.1·sum(F_i²)/sum(F_i), using the successful F_i values. If it has successful CR values, set mu_CR=0.9·mu_CR+0.1·mean(CR_i). Keep mu_F clipped to [0.05,1] and mu_CR clipped to [0,1]. If there are no successes, retain both means. Before a generation, save the global-best score. After it, reset the no-improvement counter only if the global best decreased by more than 1e−12·max(1,abs(saved_score)); otherwise increment the counter.

11) On reaching the n-specific stagnation limit, restart if the restart allowance remains. Sort the current population by exact score. Build a new population with global_best_h first and then the best distinct current members until max(2,P//4) elite slots are filled; define distinctness by maximum absolute coordinate difference at least 1e−10. Fill about 70% of the remaining slots using projections of global_best_h plus independent Gaussian noise, with sigma cycling through 0.04, 0.12, and 0.30 by restart number. Fill the rest with projected rng.random(n) vectors. Use the same 30P proposal cap and feasible-copy fallback if necessary. Reuse scores for retained elites and compute exact scores for immigrants; update the global best if an immigrant improves it. Clear the archive, reset mu_F=0.55 and mu_CR=0.70, reset the no-improvement counter, and increment the restart count. If the stagnation limit is reached after all allowed restarts have been used, terminate the generation loop. Otherwise stop after G generations. All restart, mutation, and adaptation operations execute inside run; none require external tuning or feedback.

12) Isolate failures. A malformed proposal, projection failure, nonfinite score, or exception while constructing or scoring one trial skips that trial and preserves the current feasible population member. If an unexpected exception interrupts the search, retain the latest valid global best and the parent fallback. Before returning, reproject global_best_h, check feasibility, and recompute its exact score. Compare it with the separately retained validated parent (or uniform fallback) by recomputed exact scores and keep the lower-scoring feasible candidate. If the search candidate fails any final check, return the fallback.

4. Search choices and useful variations

The default is the three-regime P and G schedule in section 3, with current-to-pbest/1 mutation, p_fraction=0.20, mu_F=0.55, mu_CR=0.70, c=0.10, a 0.1 Cauchy scale, a 0.1 normal crossover perturbation, and the stated stagnation restarts. At the supplied n=45 resolution, this uses 96 members and at most 300 generations, while retaining the parent and exact-scoring every projected trial. These are fixed defaults and require no preliminary experiments.

A coder may choose nearby explicit alternatives when writing the one program: P=72–128 and G=200–400 for n≤64; P=40–72 and G=100–200 for 65≤n≤128; and P=16–24 and G=20–40 for larger n. Usable parameter ranges are p_fraction 0.10–0.25, c=0.05–0.20, mu_F=0.45–0.70, mu_CR=0.55–0.85, initial perturbation scales 0.03–0.10 and 0.15–0.35, and two to four restarts for small n. The stated defaults are preferred when the program has no internal reason to vary them. If a different configuration is selected, it must still specify finite generation and restart caps and use the exact acceptance, projection, and fallback rules. Do not change resolution or claim that any parameter setting reaches the target score.

Correctness requirements that cannot vary are the complete 2n−1 finite-support lag objective, using the parent’s resolution when valid, keeping every stored population vector feasible, joint box-and-sum projection, exact score comparisons, and retaining a validated parent as fallback. The only result-dependent adaptation is the specified successful-parameter update and stagnation restart, both executed inside the generated program.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

The population and archive require O(Pn) storage; the exact correlation output and temporary vectors require O(n) additional storage. At n=45, P=96 is small. Do not allocate an n-by-n matrix, a lag-by-coordinate Jacobian, or a dense quadratic form. The exact np.correlate score costs O(n²) work per candidate and O(n) output memory. The configured trial-evaluation caps are approximately P·G plus initialization and at most one population’s worth of immigrants per restart: about 96·300 for the supplied-size regime, 56·150 for the medium regime, and 20·32 for the largest regime. These caps keep work bounded on one CPU; early stagnation termination can reduce it.

Use float64 throughout. Check finiteness after reading the parent, generating a donor, projecting, and computing a score. The projection clips only as part of the joint threshold formula and adjusts residual mass only through available box capacity. Every accepted population member and archive member must pass check_feasible. If exact scoring raises or returns a nonfinite value, reject that proposal. If a restart cannot produce distinct members within its attempt cap, use feasible copies rather than invalid vectors. Preserve the last valid global best on any search failure. The finite generation, fill-attempt, mutation-retry, and restart limits guarantee termination. Differential evolution is stochastic and nonconvex; neither convergence to a global optimum nor a particular score is asserted.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated program must expose run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level and return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points). Use the runtime initial_h_values global when it passes validation, without embedding or reconstructing its values in source. Keep all helpers top-level and perform parent validation, feasible population construction, projection, exact objective evaluation, candidate acceptance, adaptation, restarts, exception recovery, and fallback selection when the harness executes the program.

Immediately before return, require h_values to be a finite one-dimensional float64 NumPy array with length n_points, entries in [0,1], and sum within 1e−10·max(1,n_points) of n_points/2. Recompute c5_bound using max(np.correlate(h_values,1.0−h_values,mode='full'))·(2.0/n_points), require a finite result, and set n_points=int(len(h_values)). Select the search result only if it passes these checks and has a lower recomputed exact score than the validated parent fallback; otherwise return the fallback. If no parent was valid, the fallback is the uniform length-45 vector and its score is computed by the same exact formula. Return no surrogate score or asserted target value.
